title: Ashvaghosha himself
hookLine: a brahmin-born poet and monk, remembered also for the poem of Nanda

cards: For weeks now, there's been a voice behind every scene. The king's fear in the palace. The worms in the plowed field.
The gates swinging open without a sound. Mara's flowers. The long night under the tree.
Someone chose every one of those pictures, and the words to hold them. His name is Ashvaghosha. And here's the honest part: we know very little about him.
We have a short signature at the end of his poems, a handful of later stories, and the poems themselves.

teach.b: First, the signature. At the close of his other long poem, the author names himself: Ashvaghosha of Saketa, son of a woman named Suvarnakshi, a monk, a great poet and speaker.
His town, his mother's name, and that he wore the robe. Not much more. Second, the brahmin.
Later tradition says he was born a brahmin and trained in the old learning before he became a follower of the Buddha. His poems seem to agree.

They are full of the old kings, sages and heroes of the Indian epics, used the way a well-read writer drops in names a learned audience will know. He doesn't throw that learning away. He puts it to work.
Third, the poem of Nanda. His other surviving poem tells of Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, newly married to a beautiful wife, Sundari, and deeply in love.
The Buddha brings him into the order, and Nanda is miserable, thinking only of her.
The poem follows him patiently, through longing, through a strange journey to see heavenly women, and on, step by step, until he lets go of craving altogether and finds peace.
It's a poem about someone who did not want to be a monk, and how he got there anyway. Fourth, the monk who wrote.
Put the pieces together and you get an unusual figure: a monk who lived by a discipline of simplicity, and who also wrote richly ornate verse. He didn't see those as opposites.
A poet monk. Tomorrow, in his own words, why.

how: Ashvaghosha's poems are read today in Sanskrit classes and in translation by students of Buddhism and of Indian literature, and the story of Nanda is retold in Buddhist teaching about craving and letting go.

o: the poet monk who wrote the Buddha's life in verse
the king who paid for the poem to be written
the Buddha's half-brother who became a monk

games.q: you're Nanda. newly married, deeply in love, and now you're a monk. all you can think about is her. what does the poem do with you?
o: follows you patiently, step by step, to peace.
games.why: the whole poem is Nanda's slow road from longing, through a journey to see heavenly women, to letting go of craving.

practice: Choose one verse you love, a line from a sacred text, a poem from school, or one of these weeks' scenes in your own words, and say it aloud, slowly, once. Listen to how it sounds in the room, then sit with the quiet that follows.

wordCard.voice: Ashvaghosha himself. A monk from Saketa, brahmin-born, tradition says, who wrote the life of the Buddha and the poem of Nanda in verse. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a poet monk. A simple robe and rich verse, with no quarrel between them. See you tomorrow.
